feedback: If stages are out of order, highlight that burial must come before layers build up and before rock forms.
If a footprint is sorted as a body fossil, clarify it records activity, not the organism's body, so it is a trace fossil.
If 'days' or 'years' is chosen for timescale, restate that fossilisation takes a very long time — millions of years.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the ordered sequence, the body-vs-trace distinction, and the vast timescale.
learnerActions: Put the five fossilisation stages in order: organism dies → buried quickly in mud/sand → layers build up and press down → sediment turns to rock over millions of years (shape preserved) → rock exposed and fossil found.
Sort example cards into body fossils (shell, bone) versus trace fossils (footprint, imprint).
Answer how long fossils take to form: days, years, or millions of years (millions of years).
activities.title: Sequence and sort the fossil facts

feedback: If the learner says it's the 'very same shell unchanged', explain the shape is preserved but the material is often replaced and turned to rock over time.
If the learner implies all dead things fossilise, note fossils are rare — they need quick burial in the right conditions; most things rot away.
If the timescale is left out, prompt for how long it takes (millions of years).
activities.intendedInsight: A full explanation names burial in sediment, layers building up, sediment turning to rock over millions of years with the shape preserved, and why fossilisation is rare.
learnerActions: In your own words, retell the fossil-formation sequence in order, from the organism dying to the fossil being found.
Explain why most dead things — like leaves that fall in a park every autumn — do NOT become fossils.
State what has to happen to the dead animal or plant first, before it can become a fossil.
Describe whether a shell fossil found in rock is the unchanged original shell or something else, and how a shell ended up inside rock.
activities.title: Retell the fossil story and explain the conditions

feedback: Discuss: the plaster isn't the shell, but it kept its shape — like how rock keeps a fossil's shape even when the original material changes.
Note the limits: this takes minutes, while real fossilisation takes millions of years and happens inside hardening sediment, not plaster.
activities.intendedInsight: The surrounding material can keep the SHAPE of an object even after the original is gone — a concrete analogy for how rock preserves a fossil's shape.
learnerActions: Press a shell firmly into clay or plasticine to leave a clear imprint, then remove the shell.
Pour plaster into the imprint and let it set.
Lift out the plaster and compare its shape to the original shell.
activities.title: Plaster cast of a shell (hands-on)

feedback: Connect the dig back to the process: 'This fossil formed through burial and millions of years before it could be dug out.'
activities.intendedInsight: Fossils are embedded in rock and uncovered by excavation; this adds realism to the 'exposed and found' stage.
learnerActions: After a fossil has formed, rotate the rock and carefully extract the fossil from it in a 3D dig.
Observe how the fossil sits embedded in the surrounding rock.
activities.title: 3D excavation (optional engagement extra)
